                                                                                                   ENG518...…….
                                                     Lecture: 22

Why do a review of research

       Assessment of the current state of research on a topic
       Identification of the experts on a particular topic
       Identification of key questions about a topic
       Determination of methodologies used in past studies of the same or similar topics.

                                                     Lecture: 23

An author basically looks for eight things when summarizing the main body of the study

   1. The focus of the study
   2. The research question
   3. The hypothesis
   4. The size of the sample and important characteristics such as age and gender
   5. The variables in the study such as:
       Observational
       Independent
       Dependent
       Moderating
   6. The procedures followed
   7. The conclusion(s) that the researcher draws from the findings
   8. Any other observations you have made

                                                     Lecture: 24

Outline for the review of research/ Criteria for the main body of the text

I. Introduction

       The research question that your review addresses.
       The importance of the topic.
       Historical background of the topic (theory, methodological issues, previous reviews, etc.).
       The goal of your review. How you plan to add to the theory and information already available.

II. Method section: Details regarding the makeup of the review.

       What years are covered?
       What preliminary sources were used to locate the studies?
       What keywords guided your search?
       Criteria for deciding which studies to review.
            Description of the constraints that limited your selection.
            Rationale for choosing these constraints.
       What studies were excluded and why?

III. Results section: Studies summarized.

       An overview of what studies will be discussed and their relation to one another and the review as a whole.
       At least one paragraph for each study summarizing the following:
            The main point of the study.
            The question(s)/hypothesis being studied.
            Samples used and how they were chosen
            Procedure(s) used
            General findings (results).
            Author’s interpretations/applications of the findings.

                                                                                                               2
                                                                                                     ENG518...…….
            Any concerns to which you might want to alert the reader.

IV. Discussion section

       Give an overview of major results of your review.
       Compare/contrast the results between studies.
       Provide possible reasons for any differences.
       Relate results to any theoretical issues you mentioned in the introduction.
       Compare with past reviews if any exist.
       Explain any difference in findings with past reviews.
       Offer application of findings toward future research.

Preparing your own review of research literature

You are to review whatever number of studies you find relevant in the space allowed. You are to develop an overall
picture of what is being studied in your chosen area.

                                                     Lecture: 25

Quantitative research has come mainly from the field of psychology, where there has been heavy emphasis on the use
of statistics to make generalizations from samples to populations. It is characterized by the use of numbers as its data.

It produces numerical data and hard facts. It aims at establishing cause and effect relationship between two variables by
using mathematical, computational and statistical methods. The research is also known as empirical research.

Qualitative research has originated with anthropologists and sociologists who rely heavily on verbal description rather
than numbers. It is characterized by verbal descriptions as its data.

It is used to gain an in-depth understanding of human behavior, experience, attitudes, intentions, and motivations, on
the basis of observation and interpretation. The researcher gives more weight to the views of the participants.

Misunderstanding regarding the differences between qualitative and quantitative approaches

       Qualitative research does not use any numbers or statistics
       Qualitative is a theoretical, whereas the quantitative is not

Case study is done to shed light on a phenomenon, which is the processes, events, persons, or things of interest to the
researcher. Examples of phenomena are programs, curricula, roles, and events. Once the phenomenon of interest is
clarified, the researcher can select a case for intensive study. A case is a particular instance of the phenomena.

                                                     Lecture: 26

Dimensions of qualitative methods

       Understanding context
       Understanding people
       Understanding interaction

Terms used in qualitative data analysis:

       Theory: a set of statements that is developed through a process of continued abstractions
       Characteristic: a single item or event in a text
       Coding: the process of attaching labels to lines of text
       Coding sorts: compilation of similarly coded blocks of text

                                                                                                               3
                                                                                                     ENG518...…….
Important concepts in designing qualitative research

        Natural setting
        Holism
        Human as a research instrument
        Redundancy

Steps in qualitative data analysis

    1.   Organize the data

Q#01: Three types of case study?
    1) Illustrative Case Studies

Typically utilizing one or two instances

    2) Exploratory (or pilot) Case Studies

for large scale studies

    3) Cumulative Case Studies

aggregate information from several sites

    4) Critical Instance Case Studies

Unique cases

Q#02: What is In-text citation?

An in-text citation is a way to credit the original source of information within the body of your
writing. It briefly identifies the source by including the author's last name and year of
publication (APA) or the author's name and page number (MLA), depending on the citation
style used.

Why Use In-Text Citations?

    To avoid plagiarism
    To give credit to the original author
    To support arguments with credible sources

Q#03: Use computer software for research study?

   ❖ Data Collection & Organization
   ❖ Statistical Analysis
   ❖ Referencing & Citation
   ❖ Writing & Formatting
   ❖ Plagiarism Checking
   ❖ Visualization
   ❖ Literature review management

Q#04: Components of research proposal?

   ➢ The problem and statement of the problem
   ➢ The review of literature or theoretical framework of the study
   ➢ The hypotheses and objectives
   ➢ The methodology and procedure of the study
   ➢ Educational implications or significance of the problem
   ➢ Definitions, assumptions and delimitations
   ➢ A tentative structure of the report
   ➢ Bibliography
   ➢ Time frame
Q#05: What are the tips for best research design?

A well-structured research design ensures accuracy, reliability, and meaningful results. Here are
key tips to create an effective research design:

   ➢ Clearly Define Your Research Problem & Objectives
   ➢ Choose the Right Research Methodology
   ➢ Select an Appropriate Sampling Strategy
   ➢ Ensure Data Collection is Reliable & Valid

   ➢ Consider Ethical Considerations
   ➢ Plan for Data Analysis
   ➢ Minimize Bias and Errors
   ➢ Maintain Flexibility
Q#06: What is literature review for reference?

A literature review for reference refers to a section in a research paper, thesis, or academic
work that surveys existing studies, books, articles, and other scholarly sources relevant to a
specific topic. It provides an overview, synthesis, and critical evaluation of prior research to
establish the foundation for a new study.

Components of a Literature Review:

   ➢ Introduction
   ➢ Method
   ➢ Results
   ➢ Discussion.
Q#07: How we add comments in note?

Adding comments in a note depends on the format and platform you're using. Here are a few
common ways:

   ➢ Handwritten Notes
   ➢ Digital Notes (MS Word, Google Docs, etc.)
   ➢ PDF Files
   ➢ Note-Taking Apps (OneNote, Evernote, Notion, etc.)
Q#08: What are the Steps of case study?

Essential steps required to be taken

   ➢ Status of the situation or unit of attention
   ➢ Collection of data, examination and history
   ➢ Diagnosis and identification of casual factors
   ➢ Adjustment, treatment and therapy (treatment)
   ➢ Follow up program
Q#09: define Plot and setting

Plot:

The plot is the general background of the story line or literary work that presents the sequence of
events in which the characters in possible conflict are involved.

The plot is typically structured into the following elements:

   ➢ Exposition
   ➢ Rising Action
   ➢ Falling Action
   ➢ Climax
Setting:

The setting is the time frame or place in which the work takes place.

It includes:

   ➢ Physical Location
   ➢ Environment
   ➢ Time Period
Q#10: What are the Steps of survey method?

Before starting survey research, one should;

   ➢ Know what exactly do you want?
   ➢ Determine the target population
   ➢ Choose the mode of data (Direct + mail + phone + personal interview)
   ➢ Select the sample
   ➢ Prepare instrument
   ➢ Write any memo or letter?
   ➢ Train the interviewers
   ➢ Recheck carefully before you start your research
Q#11: Describe the importance of a literature review.

A literature review is an important part of research because it helps you understand what has
already been studied about a topic. It provides background information, identifies gaps in
knowledge, and ensures that your work is not just repeating what others have done. By reviewing
previous studies, you can build a strong foundation for your research, choose the best methods,
and support your ideas with existing knowledge. It also helps combine different viewpoints,
showing patterns and differences in past studies. Most importantly, a literature review justifies
why your research is needed and makes your work more credible.

Q#12: Types of In-text citation

   ➢ Parenthetical Citation
   ➢ Narrative Citation
   ➢ Direct Quote Citation
Q#13: Characteristics of action research?

Action Research is a process in which participants examine their own educational practice
systematically and carefully, using the techniques of research.

Characteristics:

   ➢ Practical and Problem-Solving Oriented
   ➢ Collaborative
   ➢ Reflective
   ➢ Cyclical Process
   ➢ Flexible and Adaptive
   ➢ Data-Driven
   ➢ Improves Practice
Q#14: Major components of a literary work?

   ➢ Setting
   ➢ Plot
   ➢ Characters
   ➢ Structure
   ➢ Style
   ➢ Atmosphere
   ➢ Theme
   ➢ Conflict
   ➢ Tone
Q#15: write Use an asterisk in the research work??

   ➢ Footnotes and Explanations
   ➢ Indicating Missing Information
   ➢ Highlighting Important Points
   ➢ Mathematical and Statistical Use
   ➢ Wildcard in Searches
Q#16: conclusion conveys the larger significance of your study explain

The conclusion of a research study is important because it highlights the larger significance of
your work.

   ➢ An overview of the study
   ➢ Overview of the findings
   ➢ Relation of findings
   ➢ Attention to limitations
   ➢ Possible applications
   ➢ Future possibilities

﻿Lecture: 22
Why do a review of research
    • Assessment of the current state of research on a topic
    • Identification of the experts on a particular topic
    • Identification of key questions about a topic
    • Determination of methodologies used in past studies of the same or similar topics.
Lecture: 23
An author basically looks for eight things when summarizing the main body of the study
    1. The focus of the study
    2. The research question
    3. The hypothesis
    4. The size of the sample and important characteristics such as age and gender
    5. The variables in the study such as:
        ◦ Observational
        ◦ Independent
        ◦ Dependent
        ◦ Moderating
    6. The procedures followed
    7. The conclusion(s) that the researcher draws from the findings
    8. Any other observations you have made
Lecture: 24
Outline for the review of research/ Criteria for the main body of the text
    I. Introduction
        ◦ The research question that your review addresses.
        ◦ The importance of the topic.
        ◦ Historical background of the topic (theory, methodological issues, previous reviews, etc.).
        ◦ The goal of your review. How you plan to add to the theory and information already available.
    II. Method section: Details regarding the makeup of the review.
        ◦ What years are covered?
        ◦ What preliminary sources were used to locate the studies?
        ◦ What keywords guided your search?
        ◦ Criteria for deciding which studies to review.
 Description of the constraints that limited your selection.
 Rationale for choosing these constraints.  What studies were excluded and why?
    III. Results section: Studies summarized.
        ◦ An overview of what studies will be discussed and their relation to one another and the review as a whole.
        ◦ At least one paragraph for each study summarizing the following:
 The main point of the study.
 The question(s)/hypothesis being studied.
 Samples used and how they were chosen
 Procedure(s) used
 General findings (results).
 Author’s interpretations/applications of the findings.
 Any concerns to which you might want to alert the reader.
    IV. Discussion section
        ◦ Give an overview of major results of your review.
        ◦ Compare/contrast the results between studies.
        ◦ Provide possible reasons for any differences.
        ◦ Relate results to any theoretical issues you mentioned in the introduction.
        ◦ Compare with past reviews if any exist.
        ◦ Explain any difference in findings with past reviews.  	Offer application of findings toward future research.
Preparing your own review of research literature
You are to review whatever number of studies you find relevant in the space allowed. You are to develop an overall picture of what is being studied in your chosen area.
Lecture: 25
Quantitative research has come mainly from the field of psychology, where there has been heavy emphasis on the use of statistics to make generalizations from samples to populations. It is characterized by the use of numbers as its data.
It produces numerical data and hard facts. It aims at establishing cause and effect relationship between two variables by using mathematical, computational and statistical methods. The research is also known as empirical research.
Qualitative research has originated with anthropologists and sociologists who rely heavily on verbal description rather than numbers. It is characterized by verbal descriptions as its data.
It is used to gain an in-depth understanding of human behavior, experience, attitudes, intentions, and motivations, on the basis of observation and interpretation. The researcher gives more weight to the views of the participants.
Misunderstanding regarding the differences between qualitative and quantitative approaches
    • Qualitative research does not use any numbers or statistics
    • Qualitative is a theoretical, whereas the quantitative is not
Case study is done to shed light on a phenomenon, which is the processes, events, persons, or things of interest to the researcher. Examples of phenomena are programs, curricula, roles, and events. Once the phenomenon of interest is clarified, the researcher can select a case for intensive study. A case is a particular instance of the phenomena.
Lecture: 26
Dimensions of qualitative methods
    • Understanding context
    • Understanding people
    • Understanding interaction
Terms used in qualitative data analysis:
    • Theory: a set of statements that is developed through a process of continued abstractions
    • Characteristic: a single item or event in a text
    • Coding: the process of attaching labels to lines of text
    • Coding sorts: compilation of similarly coded blocks of text

Important concepts in designing qualitative research
    • Natural setting
    • Holism
    • Human as a research instrument
    • Redundancy
Steps in qualitative data analysis
    1. Organize the data
    2. Identify a Framework
    3. Sort data in to Framework
    4. Use Framework in descriptive analysis
    5. Second order analysis
Types of qualitative data analysis (QDA)
    • Content analysis - procedure for categorization of verbal data for the purpose of classification, summarization
    • Narrative analysis - to reformulate stories presented by people in different contexts
    • Discourse analysis - analyzing a naturally occurring talk and all types of written texts
    • Framework analysis - Transcribing & reading the data
    • Grounded theory
Lecture: 27
Traditional qualitative data analysis: a labor-intensive process
Traditionally, qualitative data analysis used to be labor intensive. Researchers were used to record the source material with a word processor. They used to make multiple photocopies of the text.
Advantages of using computer software in qualitative studies
    • Search and retrieval of data
    • Transcribing data
    • Editing the data
    • Easy storage of data
    • Coding data
    • Graphic mapping

ENG518_Glossary

1. Action research :Action research refers to a wide variety of evaluative,
   investigative, and analytical research methods designed to diagnose problems or
   weaknesses—whether organizational, academic, or instructional—and help
   educators develop practical solutions to address them quickly and efficiently.
2. APA Style :APA Style is a writing style and format for academic documents such
   as scholarly journal articles and books. ... It is described in the style guide of the
   American Psychological Association (APA), which is titled the Publication
   Manual of the American Psychological Association.
3. Bibliography :An bibliography is a list of resources with citations related to a
   particular topic or arranged thematically that include a brief descriptive or
   evaluative summary.
4. Case Study :The term case study refers to both a method of analysis and a
   specific research design for examining a problem, both of which are used in most
   circumstances to generalize across populations.
5. Data analysis :Data Analysis is the process of systematically applying statistical
   and/or logical techniques to describe and illustrate, condense and recap, and
   evaluate data.
6. Data collection :Data collection is the process of gathering and measuring
   information on variables of interest, in an established systematic fashion that
   enables one to answer stated research questions, test hypotheses, and evaluate
   outcomes.
7. Dependent Variable :The variable that depends on other factors that are
   measured. These variables are expected to change as a result of an experimental
   manipulation of the independent variable or variables. It is the presumed effect.

By ASFAND YARR

                             ENG518_Glossary

8. Historical research :One type of qualitative research is historical research,
   which involves examining past events to draw conclusions and make predictions
   about the future.
9. Hypothesis :A hypothesis is a tentative statement about the relationship between
   two or more variables. It is a specific, testable prediction about what you expect
   to happen in a study.
10. Independent Variable :The variable that is stable and unaffected by the other
   variables you are trying to measure. It refers to the condition of an experiment
   that is systematically manipulated by the investigator. It is the presumed cause.
11. Instrument and Instrumentation :Instrument is the general term that
   researchers use for a measurement device (survey, test, questionnaire, etc.). To
   help distinguish between instrument and instrumentation, consider that the
   instrument is the device and instrumentation is the course of action (the process
   of developing, testing, and using the device).
12. Interpretation of data :Interpretation of data refers to the task of drawing
   inferences from the collected facts after an analytical and/or experimental study.
13. Interviewing :An interview is a conversation for gathering information. A
   research interview involves an interviewer, who coordinates the process of the
   conversation and asks questions, and an interviewee, who responds to those
   questions. Interviews are an appropriate method when there is a need to collect
   in-depth information on people’s opinions, thoughts, experiences, and feelings.
14. Observation :Observation is a systematic data collection approach.
   Researchers use all of their senses to examine people in natural settings or
   naturally occurring situations.

By ASFAND YARR

                              ENG518_Glossary

15. Problem statement :A problem statement is the description of an issue
   currently existing which needs to be addressed. It provides the context for the
   research study and generates the questions which the research aims to answer.
16. Qualitative methods :The word qualitative implies an emphasis on the
   qualities of entities and on processes and meanings that are not experimentally
   examined or measured [if measured at all] in terms of quantity, amount, intensity,
   or frequency. Qualitative researchers stress the socially constructed nature of
   reality, the intimate relationship between the researcher and what is studied, and
   the situational constraints that shape inquiry.
17. Quantitative methods :Quantitative methods emphasize objective
   measurements and the statistical, mathematical, or numerical analysis of data
   collected through polls, questionnaires, and surveys, or by manipulating pre-
   existing statistical data using computational techniques. Quantitative research
   focuses on gathering numerical data and generalizing it across groups of people
   or to explain a particular phenomenon.
18. Questionnaire :A questionnaire is a research instrument consisting of a series
   of questions (or other types of prompts) for the purpose of gathering information
   from respondents.
19. Reliability :Reliability can be thought of as consistency. Does the instrument
   consistently measure what it is intended to measure?
20. Research :The systematic investigation into and study of materials and
   sources in order to establish facts and reach new conclusions.
21. Research design :The research design refers to the overall strategy that you
   choose to integrate the different components of the study in a coherent and logical

   way, thereby, ensuring you will effectively address the research problem; it
   constitutes the blueprint for the collection, measurement, and analysis of data.

   the purpose of making business decisions. The methodology may include
   publication research, interviews, surveys and other research techniques, and
   could include both present and historical information.
23. Research paper :A substantial piece of academic writing, usually done as a

   measured. These variables are expected to change as a result of an experimental
   manipulation of the independent variable or variables. It is the presumed effect.

By ASFAND YARR

                             ENG518_Glossary

8. Historical research :One type of qualitative research is historical research,
   which involves examining past events to draw conclusions and make predictions
   about the future.
9. Hypothesis :A hypothesis is a tentative statement about the relationship between
   two or more variables. It is a specific, testable prediction about what you expect
   to happen in a study.
10. Independent Variable :The variable that is stable and unaffected by the other
   variables you are trying to measure. It refers to the condition of an experiment
   that is systematically manipulated by the investigator. It is the presumed cause.
11. Instrument and Instrumentation :Instrument is the general term that
   researchers use for a measurement device (survey, test, questionnaire, etc.). To
   help distinguish between instrument and instrumentation, consider that the
   instrument is the device and instrumentation is the course of action (the process
   of developing, testing, and using the device).
12. Interpretation of data :Interpretation of data refers to the task of drawing
   inferences from the collected facts after an analytical and/or experimental study.
13. Interviewing :An interview is a conversation for gathering information. A
   research interview involves an interviewer, who coordinates the process of the
   conversation and asks questions, and an interviewee, who responds to those
   questions. Interviews are an appropriate method when there is a need to collect
   in-depth information on people’s opinions, thoughts, experiences, and feelings.
14. Observation :Observation is a systematic data collection approach.
   Researchers use all of their senses to examine people in natural settings or
   naturally occurring situations.

By ASFAND YARR

                              ENG518_Glossary

15. Problem statement :A problem statement is the description of an issue
   currently existing which needs to be addressed. It provides the context for the
   research study and generates the questions which the research aims to answer.
16. Qualitative methods :The word qualitative implies an emphasis on the
   qualities of entities and on processes and meanings that are not experimentally
   examined or measured [if measured at all] in terms of quantity, amount, intensity,
   or frequency. Qualitative researchers stress the socially constructed nature of
   reality, the intimate relationship between the researcher and what is studied, and
   the situational constraints that shape inquiry.
17. Quantitative methods :Quantitative methods emphasize objective
   measurements and the statistical, mathematical, or numerical analysis of data
   collected through polls, questionnaires, and surveys, or by manipulating pre-
   existing statistical data using computational techniques. Quantitative research
   focuses on gathering numerical data and generalizing it across groups of people
   or to explain a particular phenomenon.
18. Questionnaire :A questionnaire is a research instrument consisting of a series
   of questions (or other types of prompts) for the purpose of gathering information
   from respondents.
19. Reliability :Reliability can be thought of as consistency. Does the instrument
   consistently measure what it is intended to measure?
20. Research :The systematic investigation into and study of materials and
   sources in order to establish facts and reach new conclusions.
21. Research design :The research design refers to the overall strategy that you
   choose to integrate the different components of the study in a coherent and logical

By ASFAND YARR

                              ENG518_Glossary

   way, thereby, ensuring you will effectively address the research problem; it
   constitutes the blueprint for the collection, measurement, and analysis of data.
22. Research methodology :The process used to collect information and data for
   the purpose of making business decisions. The methodology may include
   publication research, interviews, surveys and other research techniques, and
   could include both present and historical information.
23. Research paper :A substantial piece of academic writing, usually done as a
   requirement for a class, in which the author does independent research into a topic

Research Methodology ENG518                                         VU

         Research Methodology
                      (ENG518)

       Lessons Compiled by
          Maha Malik

                  VIRTUAL UNIVERSITY OF PAKISTAN

                                            Lessons compiled by Maha Malik

Research Methodology (ENG518)                                                                          VU

                                                                                           Lesson-01

                                   WHAT IS RESEARCH?

Topic-001: What is Research?

        The course provides in-depth understanding of research methodologies. The focus is emphasize
each step involved in research methodology starting from locating the research problem to designing and
developing a complete research. The course will equip the students with the awareness of the distinctive
concepts of research process and their varied implementation.

The course aims to:
    understand and have an overview of the fundamentals of research methods used in the field of
       English Language Teaching (ELT)
    critically evaluate a research problem and formulate research questions and objectives for a study
       to address the issue.
    formulate (in a particular context) the major components of a research study (e.g., title, abstract,
       introduction, research design, discussion and conclusion)
    present a research proposal and critically argue to defend the research design

    Research is a systematic inquiry that investigates hypotheses, suggests new interpretations of data or
texts, and poses new questions for future research to explore (Jolla, 2015).

Research consists of:

       Asking a question that nobody has asked before;
       Doing the necessary work to find the answer; and
       Communicating the knowledge you have acquired to a larger audience.

    In practice, research methods vary widely, depending upon the academic discipline’s accepted
standards, the individual researcher’s preferences, or a particular study’s needs. Research in science and
engineering often involves conducting experiments in the lab or in the field. Research in the arts,
humanities, and social sciences may include archival work in the library or on the internet, conducting
surveys or in-depth interviews, and a wide range of creative and artistic projects- from costume design to
playwriting to curating a fine arts exhibit.

Topic-002: Definitions of research

         In the broadest sense of the word, research includes any formal gathering of data, information and
facts for the advancement of knowledge.
         Research is conducted according to the researcher’s intention, their purpose, and the paradigm
they are operating from within. While many people use the word “research” to loosely mean “gathering
information” scientists use this word in a more specific way. The term “research” in a scientific context
usually refers to the entire scientific method from start to finish.
Research adds to the scientific knowledge of the subject. According to Francis G. Cornell, it is a reliable

                              ©Copyright Virtual University of Pakistan                                  1

                                                                        Lessons compiled by Maha Malik

Research Methodology (ENG518)                                                                         VU

verifiable and exhaustive process. Research is a careful inquiry or examination in seeking facts or
principles (Clifford Woody Uof Michigan), it urges for the discovery of truth (critical thinking), defining
and redefining problems, formulating hypotheses (or suggesting solutions) collecting, organizing and
evaluating data, making deductions and reaching conclusions.
         CC Crawford says that research is simply a systematic and refined technique of thinking,
employing specialized tools, instruments, and procedures; we opt for research to obtain a more adequate
solution of a problem than would be possible under ordinary means. Encyclopedia of Social Science
defines it as the manipulation of things concepts or symbols-generalizing to extend, correct or verify
knowledge. V. Redman and A.V.H. Mory state that research is a systematized effort to gain new
knowledge. Francies Rummel discussed about research as an endeavor to discover, develop and verify
knowledge, an intellectual process which is developed over hundreds of years, ever changing in purpose
and form and always searching for truth. According to P.M. Cook, research is an honest exhaustive,
intelligent searching for facts and their meanings or implications with reference to a given problem. The
product or findings of a given piece of research should be an authentic, verifiable contribution to
knowledge in the field studied.

Topic-003: General Characteristics of Research

The characteristics of research are:
    The nature of research is systematic-logical- empirical-reductive-replicable.
    It gathers new knowledge or data from primary or first-hand sources.
    Emphasis upon the discovery of general principles
    Exact systematic and accurate investigation involved
    Uses certain valid data gathering devices
    Logical and objective
    Resists the temptation to seek only the data that support his hypotheses
    Eliminates personal feelings and preferences
    Patient and unhurried activity
    Carefully recorded and reported
    Conclusions and generalizations are arrived at carefully and cautiously

Topic-004: Functions of Research

Research is the name of seeking new knowledge for continuous improvement.
    Through research refinement and extension of knowledge happens, it provides baseline data or
       simply a picture of how things are.
    Research makes decision-making easier, concerning the acquisition of knowledge in a specific
       field
    It improves learning and teaching processes
    It improves various aspects of human life

ENG518
1. Research

A systematic inquiry aimed at discovering, interpreting, or revising facts, theories, or
applications. It involves formulating a research question, collecting data, analyzing it, and
deriving conclusions.

2. Hypothesis

A tentative statement predicting a relationship between two or more variables. It provides a focus
for research and can be tested for validity.

3. Variables

Factors or elements that can change or vary in a study. They are used to measure the relationship
or impact of one element on another.

4. Independent Variable

The variable that is manipulated or controlled by the researcher to observe its effect on the
dependent variable.

5. Dependent Variable

The outcome or the variable being tested and measured. Its changes depend on the independent
variable.

6. Moderator Variable

A variable that influences the strength or direction of the relationship between an independent
and a dependent variable.

7. Control Variable

Variables kept constant to ensure they do not affect the outcome of the study. They help isolate
the relationship between the independent and dependent variables.

8. Intervening Variable

A hypothetical variable that explains the relationship between the independent and dependent
variables. It cannot be observed directly but is inferred from the data.

9. Sampling

The process of selecting a subset of individuals from a population to represent the whole. It
makes research feasible by focusing on a manageable group.

10. Population

The entire group of individuals or items being studied, from which a sample is drawn.

11. Sample

A smaller, manageable group selected from the population to conduct research. It must represent
the population to generalize findings.

12. Qualitative Research

Focuses on understanding human behavior, beliefs, and experiences through non-numerical data
like interviews, observations, and texts.

13. Quantitative Research

Emphasizes numerical data, statistical methods, and measuring relationships between variables.

14. Basic Research

Also known as fundamental research, it seeks to expand existing knowledge without a focus on
practical applications.

15. Applied Research

Research aimed at solving specific practical problems or improving processes in real-world
settings.

16. Action Research

A participatory research approach focusing on solving specific problems within a community or
organization through active involvement.

17. Exploratory Research

Conducted to explore new areas where little knowledge exists, providing insights and generating
hypotheses for further research.

18. Confirmatory Research

Tests a specific hypothesis or theory to confirm or refute it using established methodologies.

19. Research Problem

A specific issue or question that the researcher aims to address through their study. It guides the
objectives and design of the research.

20. Research Objectives

Clear and specific goals the researcher intends to achieve. They provide direction and focus to
the study.

21. Research Design

A structured plan outlining how the study will be conducted, including methods, sampling, and
analysis.

22. Data Collection Procedures

Techniques used to gather information for analysis. Common methods include observations,
surveys, interviews, and experiments.

23. Observational Data Gathering

Involves collecting data by observing subjects in their natural or controlled environment.

24. Instrumental Data Gathering

Uses tools like surveys, questionnaires, and tests to collect data systematically.

25. Validity

The degree to which a research instrument measures what it is intended to measure. Ensures
accuracy of results.

26. Reliability

The consistency of measurement results when the same instrument or method is used repeatedly.

27. Correlation Coefficient

A statistical measure indicating the strength and direction of a relationship between two
variables. Ranges from -1 to +1.

28. Primary Research

Original research conducted to collect firsthand data through methods like experiments, surveys,
or interviews.

29. Secondary Research

Involves analyzing existing data collected by others, such as books, articles, or databases.

30. Research Paradigms

Frameworks or approaches guiding research, including positivism, constructivism, and
pragmatism.

31. Experimental Group

The group in a study that receives the treatment or intervention being tested.

32. Control Group

The group that does not receive the treatment or intervention. Used as a baseline to compare
results.

33. Literature Review

A summary and evaluation of existing research on a topic, identifying gaps and justifying the
study's purpose.

34. Position Paper

A written report presenting an argument or viewpoint on a specific issue, often based on prior
research.

35. Research Ethics

Standards ensuring the protection, privacy, and rights of participants. Includes informed consent
and avoiding harm.

36. Internal Validity

The extent to which a study accurately establishes cause-and-effect relationships without
interference from extraneous variables.

37. External Validity

The degree to which findings can be generalized to other populations or settings.

38. Null Hypothesis

A statement asserting no relationship or difference between variables. It is tested to be either
accepted or rejected.

39. Directional Hypothesis

Predicts the specific direction of the relationship between variables (e.g., positive or negative).

40. Research Proposal

A detailed plan outlining the intended research, including objectives, methodology, and
significance.

41. Sampling Techniques

Methods for selecting participants, such as random sampling, stratified sampling, and
convenience sampling.

42. Random Sampling

A probability sampling method where every individual in the population has an equal chance of
selection.

43. Stratified Sampling

Divides the population into subgroups and selects samples from each to ensure representation.

44. Convenience Sampling

Non-probability sampling where participants are selected based on availability and ease of
access.

                                                  Lecture: 01

Research - it urges for the discovery of truth (critical thinking), defining and redefining problems, formulating
hypotheses, collecting, organizing and evaluating data, making deductions and reaching conclusions.
Characteristics of research
      • The nature of research is systematic-logical- empirical-reductive-replicable.
      • It gathers new knowledge or data from primary or first-hand sources.
      • Emphasis upon the discovery of general principles
      • Uses certain valid data gathering devices
      • Logical and objective
      • Eliminates personal feelings and preferences
      • Carefully recorded and reported
      • Conclusions and generalizations are arrived at carefully and cautiously

Functions of Research

       •   Refinement and extension of knowledge happens
       •   Makes decision-making easier
       •   Improves learning and teaching processes
       •   Improves various aspects of human life

Areas of concern in ELT research

   •   Students
   •   Teachers (ES/FL)
   •   Parents
   •   Admin
   •   Stakeholders
   •   Understanding of language issues

What is ELT Research About?

   •   Language policy
   •   Practical issues
   •   Problems related to second or foreign language
   •   The preservation of endangered languages
   •   Bilingualism
   •   Multilingualism
   •   Language education
   •   Assessment and evaluation

                               ENG518_Research Methodology
                                   Quiz for Final-Term

   1. The main benefit of doing a ___________________ is to provide the consumer with a
      mosaic of what is happening concerning a given topic (Literature review)
   2. While constructing a literature review, you might realize that the differences in the samples
      used in the studies produced the differing results. (true)
   3. If you do not find that the same results are replicated over a variety of studies, you can have
      more confidence that you are on the right track. (False)
   4. Doing a ________________ is important if you plan to do a study yourself. (Research
      review)
   5. The first place to begin is searching for studies using _____________ sources.
      (Preliminary)
   6. In preparation for constructing your review of the research literature, you need to formulate
      a __________ procedure for cataloging and storing your information for each study.
      (Systematic)
   7. When you set up your database of studies for your review, enter the following use. First,
      record very accurately the last names and all initials for every author of each study. (true)
   8. If you have read a published literature review, you will have noticed that the author
      basically looks for eight things when summarizing the ____________ of the study. (Main
      body)
   9. The variables in the study can be of _______ types. (Four)
   10.The focus of the study means that the area or the issue must be ignored. (False)
   11.The headings that are used in reporting most primary research studies including
      Introduction, ___________, Results and Discussion. (Method)
   12._________ section of literature review gives the details regarding the makeup of the
      review. (Method)
   13.Description and __________ are in fact criteria for deciding which studies to review.
      (Rationale)
   14.__________ section of literature review is an overview of what studies will be discussed
      and their relation to one another and the review as a whole. (Result)
   15.______________ section of literature review compares and contrast the results between
      studies. (Discussion)
   16.The Qualitative–Quantitative continuum has received a lot of attention over the past
      __________ years, usually accompanied with much controversy. (20)
   17.Larsen-Freeman and Long (1991), who described the two terms, quantitative and
      qualitative as two ends of a __________. (Continuum)
   18.Quantitative research has come mainly from the field of ________. (Psychology)
   19.______________ research frequently uses sample strategies for generalizing findings to
      larger populations. (Quantitative)
   20._________ research works to uncover information from information – rich samples.
      (Qualitative)

What is research?
  - Research is a systematic process of investigating a topic or problem.
  - It aims to discover new knowledge, validate existing ideas, or solve
     practical issues.
  - Researchers gather data, analyze it, and draw conclusions.
General characteristics of research
  - Rigorous: Research follows a structured approach with clear steps.
  - Objective: It seeks unbiased information.
  - Replicable: Others can repeat the study to verify results.
Functions of research
  - Advancing knowledge: Research contributes to our understanding of
     ELT.
  - Improving practice: It informs teaching methods and materials.
  - Solving problems: Research addresses real-world challenges.
Specific characteristics of ELT research
  - Focuses on language teaching and learning.
  - Investigates language acquisition, classroom strategies, and learner
     needs.
Research in ELT (AL)
  - ELT research explores language teaching theories and practices.
  - It examines language skills, assessment, and teacher development.
What is ELT research about?/Why is research in ELT important?
  - Researchers identify gaps and areas for investigation.
  - They ask relevant questions to guide their studies.
Demythologizing research

  - Demystifies complex research concepts.
  - Makes research accessible to educators.
Identifying important questions in ELT
  - Researchers identify gaps and areas for investigation.
  - They ask relevant questions to guide their studies.
Classification of research
  - Descriptive: Describes phenomena (e.g., language use in classrooms).
  - Experimental: Tests hypotheses (e.g., effectiveness of a teaching
     method).
Major types of research
  - Qualitative: Focuses on understanding context and meaning.
  - Quantitative: Involves numerical data and statistical analysis.
Educational research
  - ELT research falls under educational research.
  - It informs educational policies and practices.
Scientific ways to solve problems
  - Scientists use the scientific method to solve problems.
  - It involves steps like making observations, asking questions, forming
     hypotheses, testing predictions, and iterating.
  - The goal is to find evidence-based solutions.
Characteristics of an investigator
  - Good investigators possess traits like curiosity, analytical thinking, and
     integrity.
  - They ask the right questions, avoid groupthink, and cope effectively
     with challenges.
Assortment of a problem
  - Assortment optimization is a common challenge in fields like retail,
     airlines, and healthcare.
  - It involves selecting the right mix of items to offer (e.g., products in a
     store) to maximize an objective (like revenue).
Identification of a problem
  - Problem identification is crucial.
  - It pinpoints the root cause of a dilemma and helps create a clear problem
     statement.

      - Researchers use it to focus their investigations.

   Criteria for the selection of a problem
     - A good research problem should be novel, significant, and well-
         defined.
     - It must address a real obstacle and contribute original insights.
     - Researchers should ask the right questions to tackle relevant problems.
   Defining a Problem and Formulating a Hypothesis:
     - A research problem sets the stage for investigation.
     - A hypothesis is a testable explanation related to the problem.
     - It guides research design and data collection.
   Kinds of a hypothesis and Characteristics of a good hypothesis
     - Hypotheses can be null (no effect) or alternative (predicting an effect).
     - A good hypothesis is specific, testable, and based on existing
         knowledge.
   Variables in a hypothesis
     - Variables are factors that change in an experiment.
     - Independent variables are manipulated, and dependent variables are
         measured.
   How to locate research?
Researchers use various sources:
     - Preliminary sources: Gather background information.
     - Secondary sources: Explore existing research.
   Locating primary research: exploring databases
     - Primary research involves collecting original data for a specific study.
     - To find primary sources, explore databases (like Google Scholar,
        PubMed, or Scopus).
     - Look for research articles, interviews, surveys, or experiments
        conducted by researchers themselves.
   LPR: Position papers vs primary research
     - Position papers express opinions or stances on a topic.
     - Primary research provides direct evidence (e.g., interviews, data) for
        analysis.

   - Position papers are secondary sources, while primary research is the
      raw material.
LPR: Tables of references and bibliographies
   - A reference list (bibliography) appears at the end of a research paper.
   - It includes all cited sources (primary and secondary).
   - Tables of references organize these sources for easy access.
LPR: Difference between primary & secondary sources
   - Primary sources offer firsthand information (e.g., original documents,
      data).
   - Secondary sources interpret or summarize primary material (e.g.,
      reviews, articles).
   - Both are essential for robust research.
Obtaining ELT related research articles
   - Explore ELT (English Language Teaching) journals, databases, and
      repositories.
   - Look for articles on language acquisition, teaching methods, and
      learner needs.
Journals related to ELT research
   - ELT journals publish research findings.
   - Examples: "TESOL Quarterly," "Applied Linguistics," and "Language
      Learning."
Exploring ELT research journals
   - Dive into journals to find primary research articles.
   - Learn from experts and stay updated on language teaching trends.
Sampling terminology
   - Sampling involves selecting a subset from a larger population.
   - Terms: sample, population, random sampling, and stratified sampling.
Sampling paradigms
   - Information-Rich Paradigm: Focuses on detailed data from a few
      cases.
   - Representative Sampling Paradigm: Aims for a broader, balanced
      sample.
Ethics in sampling of human participants

Lesson-01

                      WHAT IS RESEARCH?

Topic-001: What is Research?
What is the main focus of the course on research methodology?
The course emphasizes each step involved in research methodology from
identifying the research problem to developing a complete research study.
What are the objectives of the course on research methodology?
The course aims to help students understand research methods in English
Language Teaching (ELT), critically evaluate research problems, formulate research
questions, and present research proposals.
How is research defined?
Research is defined as a systematic inquiry that investigates hypotheses, suggests
new interpretations of data, and poses new questions for future exploration.

What are the objectives of this research methodology course?
The course aims to help students understand fundamental research methods in
English Language Teaching (ELT), critically evaluate research problems, formulate
research questions and objectives, and develop major components of a research
study, such as title, abstract, introduction, research design, discussion, and
conclusion. It also involves presenting a research proposal and defending the
research design.
Topic-002: Definitions of research
How do scientists generally use the term "research" in a scientific context?
In a scientific context, "research" typically refers to the entire scientific method,
including all stages from start to finish.
What are some characteristics of research according to various definitions?
Research is described as a systematic and refined technique of thinking, a reliable,
verifiable, and exhaustive process, and an intellectual process that seeks truth and
new knowledge.
What is the broadest sense of the word "research" and its purpose?
In the broadest sense, research encompasses any formal gathering of data,
information, and facts to advance knowledge. It's conducted with the researcher's
intention and purpose, and it follows the scientific method from start to finish.
The purpose is to add to scientific knowledge, engage in a reliable, verifiable, and
exhaustive process, seek the discovery of truth, formulate hypotheses, collect and
evaluate data, and reach conclusions.
Topic-003: General Characteristics of Research
What are the main characteristics of research?
Research is systematic, logical, empirical, reductive, replicable, and gathers new
knowledge from primary sources. It emphasizes the discovery of general
principles and uses valid data gathering devices.
How does research eliminate personal feelings and preferences?

Research resists the temptation to seek only data that supports hypotheses,
emphasizing objective and logical investigation.
What are the key characteristics of research?
Research is systematic, logical, empirical, reductive, and replicable. It gathers new
knowledge from primary sources, emphasizes the discovery of general principles,
and involves exact, systematic, and accurate investigation using valid data
gathering devices. It maintains logical and objective standards, resists the
temptation to support only hypotheses, eliminates personal feelings and
preferences, and is a patient, unhurried activity. Research is carefully recorded and
reported, and conclusions and generalizations are made carefully and cautiously.
Topic-004: Functions of Research
What is the primary purpose of research?
Research seeks new knowledge for continuous improvement, refines existing
knowledge, and provides baseline data for decision-making.
How does research impact human life?
Research improves various aspects of human life, such as learning, teaching, and
decision-making in specific fields.
What is the primary function of research?
Research primarily seeks new knowledge for continuous improvement. It refines
and extends existing knowledge, providing baseline data and facilitating decision-
making in various fields. Additionally, research contributes to improving learning
and teaching processes and various aspects of human life.
Topic-005: Specific Characteristics of ELT Research
Why is there a substantial amount of research in ELT (English Language
Teaching)?
ELT research provides deep insight, imaginative problem-solving techniques, and a
sound philosophy to improve teaching and learning.
Is ELT research interdisciplinary, and how does it bridge different fields?

ELT research is interdisciplinary, bridging fields like psychology (e.g., motivation
and anxiety) and sociology (e.g., cultural assimilation and social varieties). It is not
as exact as physical sciences and may involve subjectivity.
Why is there a significant amount of research in English Language Teaching
(ELT)?
ELT research is extensive due to its sound philosophy, deep insights, and
imaginative problem-solving techniques. It combines theoretical and applied
research, aiming to enhance teaching and learning. ELT research, while not as
exact as physical sciences, embraces subjectivity and is not restricted to
specialists. It is an interdisciplinary field bridging psychology (e.g., motivation and
anxiety) and sociology (e.g., cultural assimilation and social varieties). It offers a
wide scope for exploration and knowledge generation.

ELT research is conducted for various stakeholders, including students, teachers,

What are the key areas of concern in ELT research?
ELT research encompasses issues related to understanding language, students,

What can be the potential topics of concern in ELT research?

                     RESEARCH VARIABLES

Topic-026: Variables in a Hypothesis
What is a variable in research?
A variable is anything that has a quantity or quality that varies.
How is a hypothesis made testable in research?
A hypothesis is made testable by using operational definitions of variables and
terms.
What are the characteristics of variables?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                            1

Variables can take different values and can increase or decrease over time.
List the types of variables.
Independent, Dependent, Moderator, Control (Intervening) variables.
What is the purpose of operational definitions in a hypothesis?
Operational definitions clarify terms used in the hypothesis, limit their meaning to
the context, provide specific definitions, ensure statement clarity, and promote
adherence to them.
Topic-027: Types of Variables
Define the independent variable.
The independent variable provides a stimulus, is measured, manipulated, or
selected, and is the cause of change in a study.
What is the role of the dependent variable?
The dependent variable is responsible for the response or output in a study and is
observed to be affected by the independent variable.
What is a moderator variable?
A moderator variable is a special type of independent variable that modifies the
relationship between other variables.
Explain the control variable.
A control variable is an experimental element that remains constant and
unchanged throughout the investigation to prevent its interference in the study.
What is an intervening variable?
An intervening variable is a hypothetical variable used to explain causal links
between other variables. It cannot be observed in an experiment.
Topic-028: Research Variables Combined
How do variables interact in research?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                             2

Independent, moderator, and control variables can interact with each other in a
research study.
In a hypothesis, what types of variables typically interact?
In a hypothesis, at least one independent variable and a dependent variable
usually interact.
What are extraneous variables in a research context?
Extraneous variables are variables other than the independent variable that could
influence the results of an experiment.
Provide an example of variables in a study and identify their types.
Among students of the same age and intelligence, skill performance is directly
related to the number of practice traits, particularly among boys but less directly
among girls.
Independent Variable: Number of practice traits
Dependent Variable: Skill performance
Moderator Variable: Sex
Control Variables: Age, intelligence
Intervening Variable: Learning (not stated)

Educational Index, MLA/APA, CIJE, SSI (Social Sci. Index), ERIC/RIE.

Secondary sources are references and summaries of primary research conducted

How can you locate primary research from secondary sources?
Valuable places to find references to primary research are literature reviews,

Topic-030: Searching Answers for Your Questions

Delimiting the research area helps narrow down the search and focus on specific

Specific keywords are essential for conducting effective searches and finding

Literature Review

      Significance – Shows the importance of your research, gives background, and identifies
       gaps in existing studies. It situates your study in the scholarly conversation.
      Three Components – Introduction, Body, Conclusion.
      Foregrounding of Writer's Voice – Your interpretation and perspective should stand
       out over citations; avoid overloading with quotes.
      Things Authors Consider – Purpose, scope, audience, currency of literature, critical
       analysis, and proper synthesis.
      Purpose of Conclusion – Summarize key points, highlight gaps, and justify the need for
       your research.
      Three Tools – Bibliographic databases (e.g., JSTOR, Google Scholar), reference
       managers (e.g., EndNote, Zotero), thematic coding software (e.g., NVivo).
      Tool/Source – Databases, academic journals, books, conference proceedings.

Experimental Research

      Method – Involves manipulation of variables, control groups, and randomization to
       determine cause-effect relationships.
      Five Designs – Pre-experimental, True experimental, Quasi-experimental, Factorial,
       Field experiments.
      Variables – Independent, Dependent, Controlled (sometimes extraneous/confounding).

Action Research

      Characteristics – Practical, problem-focused, collaborative, cyclical process, directly
       linked to professional practice.
      Components – Identifying problem, planning action, implementing action, observing,
       reflecting.
      3 Purposes – Improve practice, solve problems, develop professional understanding.
      5 Suggestions – Define a clear focus, collaborate, collect reliable data, act on evidence,
       reflect for improvement.
      Practitioner Research – Research conducted by practitioners (teachers, doctors, etc.) in
       their professional context to improve practice.

Survey Method

      First 5 Steps – Identify objectives, design the survey, choose sample, develop
       questionnaire, pilot test.

      Purpose – Collect quantitative/qualitative data on attitudes, opinions, or behaviors.
      Steps – Define problem, select sample, design instrument, collect data, analyze data,

Sampling

      Qualitative Sampling Methods – Purposive, Snowball, Convenience.

Synopsis

      Brief summary of the research problem, objectives, methodology, and significance.

Case Study

      Definition – In-depth investigation of a single case (individual, group, institution).
      Types – Intrinsic, Instrumental, Collective.
      Five Characteristics – Context-specific, multiple data sources, detailed description,
       holistic, exploratory/explanatory.

Historical-Biographical

      Approach – Uses historical facts and life histories to understand events and individuals.
      Source – Primary sources (letters, archives, interviews), secondary sources (books,
       articles).
      Old Historians – Early writers who recorded historical events without modern critical
       methods.

Qualitative Research

      Types – Ethnography, Phenomenology, Case study, Grounded theory, Narrative research.
      Five Designs – Same as above.
      Qualitative Data Analysis (QDA) – Process of coding, categorizing, and interpreting
       data.
      Terms Used – Coding, theme, category, triangulation, saturation.

      Theory and Coding – Coding identifies themes; theory explains patterns.

Reading & Note-taking

      Purpose of Reading – Gain understanding, identify gaps, support arguments.
      Three Note-taking Strategies – Summarizing, paraphrasing, annotating.
      Adding Your Own Comment – Use brackets or a separate section to record personal
       insights.
      Identifying Bias – Look for loaded language, lack of evidence, selective presentation of
       facts.

Quotations

      Use Appropriately – Quote only when wording is important; integrate smoothly; cite
       correctly.
      Three Uses of Quotation Marks – Direct quotes, highlighting terms, indicating titles of
       short works.

Documentation

      Strategies for Choosing Style – Field requirements, audience, publication guidelines.
      MLA Format – Author-page in-text citation, Works Cited page.
      Good Citation – Complete, consistent, accurate, with correct formatting.

Conclusion & Discussion

      Compelling Conclusion – Restates findings, emphasizes significance, suggests
       implications.
      Summarizing Conclusions – Be concise, link to objectives, indicate contributions.
